entry.evidence: the following three problems still exist for all the earlier studies on gravity variations in SE-AK

steps.action: Names three problems with earlier SE-AK gravity work: 3-year series too short for precise rates, degraded PDIM model resolution, and no GIA model built from AG rates themselves.
steps.quote: First, a 3-year duration is too short to obtain precise AG variation rates.

steps.action: Measured absolute gravity with the FG5-111 at six points every June in 2012, 2013 and 2015 (about 2 days and 100 sets per point), relocating the MGVC point by about 5 m.
steps.quote: We conducted repeated AG measurements at six gravity points

steps.action: Found residual diurnal and semidiurnal signals after the Inazu ocean-tide loading correction at seashore points and added a sine-curve regression to estimate yearly mean gravity.
steps.quote: we found that diurnal and semidiurnal gravity changes persisted in the time series of gravity sets at seashore AG points

steps.action: Reprocessed the 2006-2008 AG data with the same procedure to build a consistent 2006-2015 data set, and noted the 2012 RUSG value was corrupted by a Superspring failure.
steps.quote: we reprocessed past AG data collected from 2006 to 2008 (Sun et al. 40; Sato [...] ) using the same procedures as above

steps.action: Computed nuisance gravity signals to remove: hydrological loading and attraction from GLDAS-2.1 with 1066A Green's functions, and coseismic changes from the 2012 Haida Gwaii and 2013 Craig earthquakes (Okubo theory, Lay et al. slip models).
steps.quote: we estimated gravity variations due to hydrological loading (Farrell 9) and mass attraction

steps.action: Justified neglecting postseismic gravity change by checking NGL GNSS time series near the AG points for postseismic displacement.
steps.quote: no significant post-seismic displacement was detected around our AG points in the SE-AK area

steps.action: Estimated gravity rates at each point by weighted least squares on the corrected 2006-2015 AG (weights from SD and UC), with a step term at MGVC and the 2012 RUSG value excluded.
steps.quote: We calculated a new gravity variation rate at each gravity point from the corrected AG from 2006 to 2015

steps.action: Compared the updated rates with Sun et al. 2010 and Sato et al. 2012: smaller errors at most points and rates smaller by up to 2.8 µGal/yr, but a doubled error at MGVC; noted the spatial pattern matches uplift.
steps.quote: Our variation rates were estimated with smaller errors (see the right side of Fig. 5) than those obtained in earlier studies

steps.action: Computed the global past ice melting (GPIM) gravity rate with ICE-6G_C and VM5a load Love numbers from ALMA (incompressible Maxwell Earth, nmax=180).
steps.quote: using the global historical deglaciation model ICE-6G_C (Peltier et al. 29)

steps.action: Checked the computed Love-number behaviour and the gravity/uplift ratio against the Bouguer value and published results (Olsson et al. 2015).
steps.quote: All of these characteristics about the load Love numbers agree well with past studies

steps.action: Designed a chi-square grid search over lithospheric thickness d and upper mantle viscosity η for the regional and local post-LIA loads (RPIM/LPIM), using a four-layer structure from Sato et al., separate from the GPIM structure.
steps.quote: we determine optimum parameters for the structure via the following grid search calculation

steps.action: Computed elastic loading and attraction gravity rates of present-day ice melting (PDIM) from merged high-resolution UAF07 and UAF05 models.
steps.quote: We merged two PDIM models to calculate the PDIM-derived gravity variations

steps.action: Tested the sensitivity of the PDIM elastic term to using a PREM instead of a 1066A Green's function (difference up to 0.13 µGal/yr).
steps.quote: This difference value is only 3.7 % of the observed gravity variation rate at a maximum

steps.action: Ran a coarse then a fine grid search: χ² minimum 3.39 at d=55 km and η=1.2×10^19 Pa s, 68.27% confidence ranges 47-64 km and 0.5-2.0×10^19 Pa s, χ²min close to the 4 degrees of freedom.
steps.quote: an additional grid search calculation with smaller grid widths

steps.action: Compared the AG-derived parameters with GNSS-based estimates (Sato et al. 2011; Hu and Freymueller 2019): consistent, with narrower error ranges than Hu and Freymueller.
steps.quote: are consistent with those determined in earlier studies using GNSS data (Sato et al. 33; Hu and Freymueller 13)

steps.action: Derived the Love numbers of the optimum model and contrasted them with VM5a: stronger response to young unloading, similar gravity/uplift ratio.
steps.quote: the structure of the Earth of our optimum model responds to the past ice unloading of

steps.action: Compared calculated with observed gravity rates per site: all agree within error, RMS 0.36 µGal/yr against 1.06 µGal/yr in earlier studies; MGVC differs from EGAN because of the PDIM attraction term.
steps.quote: the root-mean-square (RMS) difference was calculated to be approximately 0.36

steps.action: Diagnosed a likely sign error in the PDIM attraction term of Sato et al. 2012; reversing it brings their rates within 0.3 µGal/yr RMS of this study's.
steps.quote: if we correctly recalculate the total gravity variation rate of Sato et al. (34) by reversing the sign of

steps.action: Predicted vertical uplift at 99 GNSS stations from the AG-derived model and compared with observed rates: residual mean −0.21 mm/yr, SD 4.20 mm/yr.
steps.quote: To verify our rheological model in terms of ground deformation, we calculate the rate of vertical ground deformation

steps.action: Estimated raw, total, viscous and elastic gravity/uplift ratios from observed and calculated rates at the six AG–GNSS pairs (viscous −0.168 observed, −0.171 calculated µGal/mm).
steps.quote: we quantified the ratio values of gravity variation to vertical ground deformation in the SE-AK area

steps.action: Compared the SE-AK viscous ratio with values for Antarctica, Greenland and Fennoscandia (Wahr 1995; Olsson 2015) and attributed the larger magnitude to more recent melting.
steps.quote: The absolute value of the viscous ratio in SE-AK was larger than those in other GIA regions

steps.action: Explained the observed–calculated elastic ratio mismatch at RUSG, BRMC and HNSG by auxiliaries (fewer AG data; the 35 km AG–GNSS offset) rather than by revising the model.
steps.quote: may be related to a systematic error in the observed gravity variation rate

steps.action: Derived Bouguer-gradient expectations (upper-mantle density for the viscous ratio, crustal density for the elastic ratio) to interpret the two ratios.
steps.quote: the ratio of the gravity variation to the vertical displacement can be approximately calculated by the Bouguer’s gravity gradient

steps.action: Tested an empirical elastic/viscous separation method at GBCL (agrees) and MGVC (fails because of PDIM attraction).
steps.quote: this empirical method is valid only when the PDIM attraction effect is small

steps.action: Varied the PDIM scale factor from 0.5 to 2.0 (d changes by only 3 km) and emulated compressibility by scaling RPIM/LPIM by 1.27 (optimum d=60 km, η=1.6×10^19 Pa s, confidence ellipses not overlapping).
steps.quote: the model parameters were robustly determined in this study to be

steps.action: Kept the AG-derived rheology d=55 (+9/−8) km and η=(1.2 +0.8/−0.7)×10^19 Pa s under the incompressible assumption, consistent with gravity and GNSS data.
steps.quote: we succeeded in obtaining a robust rheological model for SE-AK, which agrees with both of gravity and crustal deformation data

tree.answer: Gravity decrease and uplift from post-LIA GIA and PDIM in SE-AK, already established by earlier GNSS and AG work
Gravity rates observed directly by AG; rheology (d, η) is latent
Precise AG rates and AG-only rheological parameters to compare with GNSS-based models
No rival hypotheses; only alternative model configurations (Green's function, PDIM scale, compressibility)
Not applicable; no rivals with distinct predictions
Conditions found: natural loading, sampled by yearly June campaigns

tree.question: 6b
tree.answer: Six sites over six campaigns; 99 GNSS stations as independent data
Robust to PDIM scale and Green's function choice; the compressibility emulation shifts the optimum outside the incompressible confidence ellipse
Estimate kept, consistent with GNSS-based rheology and GNSS uplift

end.claim: From 2006-2015 absolute gravity rates alone, SE-AK lithospheric thickness is 55 (+9/−8) km and upper mantle viscosity (1.2 +0.8/−0.7)×10^19 Pa s (incompressible Earth), consistent with GNSS-based estimates and with observed uplift at 99 GNSS stations.

decisive_move.sentence: The new 2012-2015 FG5 campaigns extended the AG series from 3 to 10 years, giving rates precise enough to constrain d and η; without them, no AG-based rheology would exist.

gates.evidence: The new measurements aimed at more precise rates, not at testing a stated hypothesis (§1 ¶3). The AG-derived parameters could have disagreed with GNSS-based estimates and could have failed to predict uplift at 99 GNSS stations (§5.1 ¶2, §5.4 ¶3). Nothing was fixed in advance; the grid ranges and the refinement were chosen after inspecting χ² (§5.1 ¶1).

imports.item: chi-square confidence region (Δχ²=2.30 for two parameters, 68.27%) and degrees-of-freedom plausibility check
weighted least-squares adjustment with inverse-variance weights

novelty_claims.quote: none of the earlier studies have created GIA models from the AG variation rate itself
in the case of SE-AK, the characteristics of the ratio value have not been quantitatively discussed

limits: No review file or earlier version was supplied, so no review sequence is coded. Sub-claims and their statuses: the viscous ratio (−0.168 observed, −0.171 calculated µGal/mm) is estimate_with_resolution, and the attribution of its larger magnitude to recent melting is best_explanation; the elastic ratio agrees with calculation only at three of six sites, so it reaches no conclusion at RUSG, HNSG and BRMC; PDIM acceleration could not be confirmed (no_conclusion), because the data are weakly sensitive to PDIM; the Sato et al. 2012 sign error is best_explanation ('may be caused'). The headline estimate depends on the incompressible assumption: the emulated compressible optimum lies outside the incompressible confidence ellipse (§6.3 ¶2). Only six rates constrain two parameters (4 degrees of freedom). The MGVC step is poorly constrained (+3.53±7.01 µGal), and RUSG and BRMC have fewer data. All other layer parameters are fixed to the Sato et al. structure, and the grid-search ranges are not justified. The GNSS check relies largely on campaign rates from earlier studies, partly the same data that informed the GNSS-based models it is compared with (inference). The 'robustness' language rests on fits to the same six rates (inference).

disagreements.support: Ten-year reprocessed series gives smaller rates (by up to 2.8 µGal/yr) with smaller errors at most points.
disagreements.quote: At most of the AG points, the updated gravity variation rates are smaller by up to 2.8

disagreements.support: Back-calculating Sato's attraction term gives values anticorrelated with this study's; reversing its sign matches within 0.3 µGal/yr RMS.
disagreements.quote: may be caused by the incorrect sign of the attraction effect of the PDIM in the estimation of Sato et al. (34)

disagreements.support: The AG grid search gives narrower error ranges, attributed to one fewer free parameter.
disagreements.quote: Our error ranges are smaller than those of Hu and Freymueller (13) by about 32 and 50 %

disagreements.support: Varying the PDIM scale factor does not change the AG-derived parameters, so AG data cannot confirm the acceleration.
disagreements.quote: the acceleration of PDIM cannot be confirmed from our AG data set (Table 2)

disagreements.target: Sun et al. 2010 (separation of elastic and viscoelastic parts)
disagreements.support: The paper separates the ratios using modelled PDIM terms where Sun et al. failed.

disagreements.target: Wahr et al. 1995; Olsson et al. 2015 (viscous gravity/uplift ratio −0.15 to −0.16 µGal/mm)
disagreements.support: The SE-AK viscous ratio is larger in magnitude, explained by more recent melting near the sites.
disagreements.quote: The absolute value of the viscous ratio in SE-AK was larger than those in other GIA regions

disagreements.target: Incompressible-Earth GIA models (Sato et al. 2011; Hu and Freymueller 2019; this study)
